title: On “Godot” pronunciation: @ @Joe Weinberg #theatre #broadway #westend...
transcript: How do you pronounce the title of this famous Greek tragedy currently playing on Broadway? I did another video recently about this other current play, revival on Broadway, which I'll link in the caption. Because they chose to use the pronunciation waiting for GOD-oh instead of waiting for guh-DOT Now we're facing a very similar situation with this new version of a classic story that's coming over from the UK so the way that we say this in US English is EH-di-pus, but in the UK they say EE-di-pus, and because this is a British production, they say EE-di-pus in the show itself, or so I'm told. I'm saying it next week. And that puts us as American audiences in a slightly odd position, because if we say EE-di-pus, it feels like we're mispronouncing the name, but if we say EH-di-pus, it feels like we're mispronouncing the title of this specific production. With waiting for Godot, it was a little more simple in my opinion, because even in America, it is often pronounced GOD-oh instead of guh-DOH, especially in more academic circles, and even in some of the more high profile productions we've had in the US. But with this one, it feels a little more clearly drawn across geographical lines. I don't speak Greek. I tried to look up what the original Greek pronunciation is and I had a little bit of trouble, but I found this old Reddit thread from like nine years ago where the responses seem to indicate that it was probably a little closer to EE-di-pus, at least in modern Greek, not necessarily in ancient Greek. But I really don't know about all that. If any Greek people or scholars wanna chime in in the comments, feel free. But either way, both of these anglicized pronunciations have clearly been widely adopted, colloquially. So even if one of them is technically closer to the original Greek, by that colloquial standard, neither one is incorrect. So if you see any videos on this app of people pronouncing it EE-di-pus, maybe don't make nasty comments if you don't know what you're talking about.
